tldr: Your network is almost entirely SLPs, which is why nobody in it can refer you. The people who already hold your target title sit in three places: the subreddit for that job, the professional community that serves it, and the companies on your list. LinkedIn is how you turn any of them into a name.

blocks.text: Everyone you could call right now works in speech. That is not a personal failing, it is what twelve years inside one profession does to a contact list, and it is the reason the advice to just network lands so badly. You are not short of social skills. You are short of people who work somewhere else.
Start with the people you already know outside speech

Before a single stranger, list the people in your life who work somewhere else: a partner's colleagues, a college friend in tech, the neighbour who sells software, a former classmate who left the field. A referral from someone who can vouch for you as a person carries more than any message to a stranger, and these people already will. The ask is small and specific, and it never asks for a job.

items: **Your grad cohort.** SLP programs are small and the cohorts stay findable. Five years out, some of them are in health-tech, ed-tech, device companies and pharma. Search the program name on LinkedIn and read where people went before you write to anyone.

**The reps who walk into your building.** The AAC device rep, the EMR trainer who ran your go-live, the feeding-product rep, the ed-tech rep who sold your district its screening platform. They hold the jobs on your map, they already know you, and taking your call is part of their job.

**The ones who already left.** The CF you supervised who never came back, the colleague who went to a vendor, your own CF supervisor if they moved on. They are the warmest cold message you will ever send.
**People who sell you things outside work.** Your realtor, your insurance agent, the person who did your taxes. They talk to everyone and they like being asked.
**Anyone you worked with before grad school.** They never knew you as an SLP, which is the point.

blocks.title: The warm ask
blocks.text:
I'm looking at [target title] roles, and I know you've been at [company] a while. Could you tell me what the [title] there actually does day to day? And if there's someone doing it you'd trust me to talk to, I'd love fifteen minutes with them.

No job ask. I'm working out whether it fits before I go further.

Say the title. People do not guess on your behalf, and "anything outside the clinic" gives them nothing to remember you by. When they can't help, ask who else they know who works somewhere interesting. That second name is usually the one that matters.

If you honestly have not decided between two titles, say both and stop there. "I'm looking at clinical liaison and customer success, and I'm trying to work out which" gives them two things to remember. "Something outside the clinic" gives them nothing.
Where the ones who left actually went

When we read a hundred threads looking for where SLPs go for this, the same answer kept coming back, and it was not a public forum. It was private Facebook groups, named again and again by people who had already got out.
The teacher transitioning groups on facebook are better. That's how I got out.

Groups like SLP alternatives and job transitions, Alternative Careers for Introverted SLPs, and the teacher-transition groups are closed and not indexed by search. That is exactly why you have not found them: they cannot be read from the outside, and you have to request to join and wait. Do that today rather than in week eight, because approval can take a week and costs you nothing while you wait.
The three places, in order

items: The subreddit for the job title, not for your profession. Search Reddit for your target title and read the complaint threads first. People describe the actual daily work there in a way no job posting will, and it is the fastest way to find out whether you want it.

The professional community for that field. Instructional Design Central for ID, Mixed Methods for UX research, the Conversation Design Institute for conversation design, HIMSS and AMIA for informatics, your local PMI chapter for project management. Most are free to read.
The 188 companies on your list. This is the one nobody else can give you, because these are health-tech and ed-tech companies that value clinical skills. Every one of them has people on LinkedIn.

blocks.text: The rooms, and the wrong room

Most SLPs go to one conference a year, and it is full of SLPs. The exhibit hall is the exception: for three days the companies on your list stand behind tables with the people who run their clinical teams, and almost nobody walks up to ask about working there. The right rooms for each path are smaller and further from home: HIMSS and AMIA for informatics, ATIA and Closing the Gap for AAC and assistive technology, DevLearn and Learning Solutions for instructional design, ISTE for ed-tech, and the state chapters of HIMSS and PMI, which cost a fraction and meet monthly.

items: Walk up to whoever is standing alone. They are relieved.
Change tables between sessions if yours has closed ranks.
Ask the organiser to introduce you, and say plainly that you are new to the field and want to meet people in it. That is what organisers are for.
Say your sixty seconds, then hand the conversation back with a question about their work. People like being the expert.
Close with "can I follow up on LinkedIn?" and do it that night.

blocks.title: The wrong room
blocks.text: The university's "alternative careers for SLPs" panel and the SLP career fair are full of people in exactly your position. Good for morale, useless for leads. Spend the evening in a room where people already have the job.
The search that finds people like you

On LinkedIn, search people rather than posts. Put a company from your list in the company filter and a term like speech-language pathologist or CCC-SLP in the keyword box. What comes back is people who did your job and now do the one you want, at a company that has hired that exact move before.

blocks.title: Two hours a week is the whole commitment
blocks.text: Read a group for a week before you post anything. When you do post, ask a question rather than introducing yourself, because an introduction asks the room for attention and a question gives someone an easy reason to reply.

items: Request to join two closed groups today and forget about them until they let you in.
Find the subreddit for your target title and read the top posts of the month.
Run one LinkedIn people search: a company from your list, plus CCC-SLP.
Save three names in the tracker. You will message them in lesson 3.3.

takeaways: Your contact list is all SLPs, so referrals have to come from people you have not met yet.
The groups where SLPs help each other leave are closed and unsearchable, which is why request to join is a week-one job.
Read the subreddit for the job title, not for your profession. The complaint threads describe the real work.
LinkedIn people search, filtered to a company on your list plus CCC-SLP, finds people who made your exact move.
Save three names before you write a single message.

Your cohort, the reps who sell into your building, and the ones who already left are warmer than any stranger. The exhibit hall is the one part of a conference full of employers rather than competitors.

tldr: The message that gets answered is short, specific, and asks for fifteen minutes about their path with no job attached. About one in four asks never gets a reply, which is a volume problem rather than a verdict. Three templates below: the first message, the single follow-up, and the thank-you that keeps the door open.

blocks.text: Referrals decide most of the successful transitions in the file, and generic applications through Indeed and LinkedIn without one are what fails. The forum threads already suspect it. Under one exit post somebody asked whether the writer had found the job through network connections or just by submitting a résumé, and some version of that question sits under most of them.
Did you find the new position through network connections or just by submitting your resume?

The ask that works is small: fifteen minutes, about how they got in, with no job attached. Expect roughly one in four to go unanswered, which means three messages is usually two conversations. Nobody in the corpus reported being annoyed by a polite ask from an SLP. What they reported, repeatedly, was being asked for their actual résumé, more than twenty times under a single post, and mostly saying yes.

Four things make a first message answerable. You name the specific move they made, so it is obvious you are writing to them and not to forty people. You ask for a fixed and small amount of time, you attach no job ask, and you make it easy to decline, which is the part most people leave out and the part that makes a stranger feel safe replying at all.

If a message to a stranger feels like too much, the connection request is the smaller door. Three hundred characters, one specific thing from their profile, one question they can answer from the sofa. Some will not accept, and that is fine; the ones who do now recognise your name.

blocks.title: The connection request, under 300 characters
blocks.text: Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] looking at [target title] roles, and I noticed you made that move from [their old setting]. I'd be glad to connect, and if you don't mind, I have one question about how the first year went.

blocks.title: The alumni version
blocks.text: Hi [Name], I saw you went through [program] too and you're now at [company]. I'm an SLP looking at [target title] roles and would love to connect. If you're open to it, I have a couple of questions about how you got there.

blocks.title: The message that doesn't get answered, and the one that does
blocks.before: Hi! I'm a speech pathologist looking to leave the field. I saw you're a Customer Success Manager. Could you tell me what a typical project looks like from start to finish, how you got the job, what the interview was like, what the salary is, and whether they're hiring? Also, would you be willing to look at my résumé?
blocks.after: Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] looking at implementation roles, and you made exactly that move. Would you have fifteen minutes in the next couple of weeks? I mostly want to know how you got the first one. No job ask, I promise.

blocks.text: The first one asks a stranger for two hours of work, attaches a résumé, and never says which title it means. The second asks for one thing, and the reader can answer it from the sofa. If Google could answer a question, don't ask a person.

blocks.title: The first message (LinkedIn or email, under 90 words)
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] and I'm looking at [target title] roles. I found you because you made the same move, and I'd rather ask you than read another article about it.

Would you be up for 15 minutes in the next couple of weeks? I mostly want to know how you got the first one and what you'd do differently. No job ask, I promise.

Either way, thank you for putting your path somewhere someone like me could find it.

[Your name]

One follow-up, seven to ten days later, and then you stop. Silence is almost always a full inbox and a bad Tuesday. A second follow-up converts almost nobody and costs you the option of asking again in six months, when you have something new to say.

blocks.title: The follow-up, once, seven to ten days later
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], floating this back up in case it got buried.

Still would love 15 minutes on how you got into [target title]. If a call is too much, I'd happily take two sentences by message instead: what surprised you most in your first three months?

Thank you either way. [Your name]

items: What did you actually do yesterday? Ask for the day, not the job description.
What did your employer require, and what did they ignore on your résumé?
Which part of clinical work turned out to be the most useful, and which part did you have to unlearn?
Which groups, newsletters or communities should I be in? One answer to this turns a fifteen-minute call into a channel that keeps sending you things.
What would you do differently if you were starting this month?
Who else should I be talking to? This is the only question that turns a conversation into an introduction, so never skip it.

blocks.title: The thank-you, same day
blocks.text:
[Name], thank you for the time. The thing I'm taking away is [one specific sentence they said, in their words].

I'm going to [the one concrete thing you'll do because of it] in the next two weeks, and I'll let you know how it lands. If [person they mentioned] would be open to the same 15 minutes, I'd be grateful for an introduction whenever it's convenient.

Thank you again. [Your name]
When they ask what you're looking for

Somewhere in the fifteen minutes they will ask. Have sixty seconds ready that says the years, the two things you'd do all day, the title, and the ask. Yours is below; fill the brackets tonight and say it out loud twice, because the first time it comes out of your mouth should not be on the call.

blocks.title: Sixty seconds, out loud
blocks.note: Your path opens first. The chips show the others.

items.liaison-ur:
I've spent [N] years as a medical SLP, most of it in [acute / inpatient rehab / SNF], where half my week was case conferences, discharge planning and explaining to families and physicians why a patient did or didn't qualify for the next level of care. I'm moving into clinical liaison work, where that's the whole job. If you know a rehab facility or home health agency that's adding a liaison, I'd like to hear about it.

For utilization review instead:

[N] years as an SLP, and the part I'm good at is the part most people hate: reading the chart, matching what was done against what the payer will cover, and writing the justification that survives an audit. I'm moving into utilization review. If you know a health plan or a UR vendor that hires therapists into reviewer roles, I'd welcome an introduction.
items.customer-success: I'm an SLP with [N] years in [setting]. The part of the job I'd keep is onboarding: getting a family or a teacher to actually use the device or the plan after I leave the room. I'm moving into customer success at a health-tech or teletherapy company, where that's the work all day. If your team is hiring an implementation or onboarding specialist, I'd like to talk.
items.informatics: I've been the SLP who ends up fixing the documentation system. [N] years in [setting], superuser through the [EMR name] rollout, built the note templates the department still uses. I'm moving into clinical informatics, the analyst or trainer side, where I translate between the clinicians and the people building the system. If your organisation has an EHR analyst or trainer opening, I'd like to be considered.
items.clinical-educator: [N] years as an SLP, and the work I loved most was teaching other clinicians to use [AAC / a speaking valve / a dysphagia protocol]. I've trained [teams / a district / nursing staff] on it. I'm moving into a clinical educator role at a company that makes the products, where teaching clinicians is the job. If you know one that's hiring, I'd like to talk.
items.instructional-design: I'm an SLP with [N] years in [setting]. I've built training for adults the whole time: in-services, onboarding for CFs, a [program] the department still runs. I've rebuilt one of them as a [Rise / Storyline] module so you can see how I work. I'm moving into instructional design. If your team needs someone who can design for adults who are busy and sceptical, I'd like to show you the module.
items.data-analysis: [N] years as an SLP, and I'm the one who kept the outcome data nobody asked for: [dismissal rates / wait times / goal attainment] by [setting], in a spreadsheet that answered questions a year later. I'm moving into healthcare analytics, and I've been learning [SQL / Tableau] to do it properly. If your quality or analytics team has an analyst opening, I'd welcome a conversation.
items.project-management: For [N] years I've run programs that had a deadline, a budget and a dozen people who didn't report to me: [a caseload of 60 across three buildings / a dysphagia program / an EMR transition]. I'm moving into project management in healthcare, and I'm working through [the Google PM certificate / CAPM]. If your organisation has a coordinator or associate PM role, I'd like to be considered.
items.content-marketing: I'm an SLP with [N] years of explaining hard clinical ideas to people who didn't ask for a glossary: families, teachers, nurses. I've started writing that down: [a blog / three samples / a newsletter]. I'm moving into health content and marketing, where translation is the whole job. If your team needs a writer who has actually done the clinical work, I'd like to send you the samples.
items.sales-bd: [N] years as an SLP. Every week I sold a treatment plan to a family that didn't want to hear it and a protocol to nurses who were too busy for it, and most of them came round. I'm moving into clinical sales for a [device / health-tech] company, where that's the work with a quota attached. If your sales team is adding a clinical specialist, I'd like to hear about it.
items.research-coordinator: [N] years as an SLP in [setting], and the part of my week that ran most like a study was the part I ran best: consenting families, following the protocol to the letter, keeping the data clean and the follow-ups on schedule. I'm moving into clinical research coordination. If your site or sponsor has a coordinator opening, I'd like to be considered.
items.leadership: I've been an SLP in [setting] for [N] years and I already run the parts of the department nobody bills for: the schedule, the coverage, the audits, the new grad who's drowning. I'm looking to move into a clinical manager or program manager role, here or somewhere like here. Who did the last two openings go to, and what did they have that I don't yet?

blocks.text: Send the thank-you the same day, then do the thing you said you would do, and tell them two weeks later that you did it. That second note is what turns a stranger into someone who forwards your résumé to a hiring manager, built out of two emails and one kept promise. Fill your setting, your target title and your name into all three templates tonight, and leave the [Name] blanks empty for the next lesson.

takeaways: Referrals decide most documented transitions, and applications sent without one are what fails.
The ask is fifteen minutes about their path with no job attached, and about one in four goes unanswered.
A first message works when it names their specific move, asks for a fixed small amount of time, and makes it easy to decline.
Follow up once, seven to ten days later, then stop.
"Who else should I be talking to?" is the question that turns a conversation into an introduction.
Have sixty seconds ready for "so what are you looking for?": years, the two things you'd do all day, the title, the ask.

tldr: Three messages, twenty minutes, tonight. About one in four gets no answer, so three sent is usually two conversations, and one conversation is worth more than another week of reading.

blocks.text: Everything in this module so far has been reading. This is the first step that involves another person, and it is the one people postpone for months. It is the easiest thing in the whole program to put off and call research, which is what research becomes once you already know the answer.

Three people, and they do not all have to be strangers. In order of value, an SLP who now holds the title you want, because they have already done the exact translation you are attempting. Then anyone who holds that title from any background, because they know what their employer actually required. Then someone at a company on your list, because a name inside beats a posting outside. The companies directory holds 188 health-tech and ed-tech companies that value clinical skills, and the deep-dive tool in 2.7 already listed the ones matching your path.

Two filters on the three names. Prefer people who have held the title for years, ideally at more than one company, because you would not ask a first-year CF what the job is like either. And skip the visible ones. The SLP with the big account and the course gets fifty messages like yours a week; the one with three hundred connections who quietly became an EHR analyst answers every one.

The conversations do two more jobs you will not notice until later. They are interview prep, because you arrive at the interview using the words people in the role actually use. And they narrow the map: after four of them you will find you have gone quiet on one path and keep asking about another. That drift is data. Cross the path off.
Why three, and why tonight

Three is a volume decision. About one in four gets no answer at all, so one message is a coin flip and three is a near-certainty of one real conversation. Sending three at once also stops you reading a single silence as a verdict on you. That is what ends most outreach after message one. Do it tonight, with the templates already filled in, because a tired brain will not do this on a Thursday three weeks from now.
burnt out brains really struggle to use executive functions, so planning and executing a career change is gonna be hard
blocks.from: an SLP, quoted in the research file

items: Set a timer for twenty minutes.
Open the three names you saved in lesson 3.1.
Paste the first-message template, change the name, the setting and the target title, and read it once for anything that sounds like a cover letter.
Send all three before the timer runs out.
Log them in the tracker with today's date, and set a reminder eight days out for the single follow-up.

blocks.title: Do not ask for a job in the first message
blocks.text: The ask is fifteen minutes about their path. A job ask puts a stranger in the position of saying no to something they cannot give you, and it is the most common reason these messages go unanswered. The referral comes later, at the end of a good conversation, when you ask who else you should be talking to.

What comes back is rarely a job. It is a description of an ordinary Tuesday, the name of the credential their employer actually cared about, a posting that is not public yet, or a second name. Any one of those is worth more than another week of reading, and by Module 5 you will need one of these people to vouch for you.

takeaways: Message three people tonight: an SLP with your target title, anyone with that title, and someone at a company on your list.
About one in four asks goes unanswered, so three sent is usually two conversations.
Sending all three at once keeps a single silence from reading as a verdict.
Never ask for a job in the first message. Ask for fifteen minutes about how they got where they are.
What comes back is a real Tuesday, a credential that mattered, an unlisted posting, or a second name.

tldr: Recruiters look you up before they call, and they find you in the first place by searching the words in the job they are filling. A clinical profile behind a translated résumé does two kinds of damage: it contradicts you, and it leaves you invisible to the search.

blocks.text: Picture the moment your application starts working. A recruiter reads the translated résumé, decides you are interesting, and does what they always do before reaching out to anybody, which is look you up. They find a headline from 2019 that says Speech-Language Pathologist, CCC-SLP, an About section about your passion for pediatric feeding, and a skills list topped by Dysphagia. Now the two documents describe different people, and the recruiter believes the free one.
The words a recruiter types

LinkedIn is a search engine whose power users are recruiters. The fields it weights hardest are the ones most SLPs leave in clinical language: headline, About, job titles, and the skills you have pinned to the top. Recruiters search the vocabulary of the role they are filling, so a profile written entirely in clinical terms never comes back in the results, which from the inside feels identical to being turned down. These are the terms worth having somewhere on your profile, by path.

items: **Customer success and implementation:** implementation specialist, onboarding, customer success manager, adoption, renewal, churn, health score.
**Project and program management:** project coordinator, program manager, stakeholder management, scope, timelines, Google Project Management certificate.
**Healthcare data:** healthcare analytics, quality improvement, dashboards, outcome data, SQL, discharge and falls data.
**Clinical liaison and utilization review:** clinical liaison, utilization review, admissions criteria, level-of-care review, referral development.

**Clinical informatics:** EHR analyst, clinical informatics, workflow optimization, go-live and activation support, CAHIMS. Name Epic only where you have real experience, since the certification requires employer sponsorship.
**Instructional design:** instructional design, learning experience designer, Articulate Storyline, Rise, ADDIE, e-learning.
**Clinical educator and trainer:** clinical educator, learning consultant, clinical trainer, product training, AAC implementation.
**Content and marketing:** content strategy, health content, clinical subject matter expert, plain-language writing, SEO.
**Medical and device sales:** clinical specialist, clinical application specialist, territory support, account management.

blocks.title: The headline, which follows you everywhere
blocks.before: Speech-Language Pathologist, CCC-SLP | Passionate about pediatric feeding and AAC
blocks.after: Implementation & Customer Success in health tech | [8] years managing [62] client accounts and their outcomes | CCC-SLP

blocks.title: A headline that comes back in the search
blocks.note: Target title first, the licence as an asset. Never "seeking opportunities" and never "former SLP" on its own, because nobody searches for either.

items.liaison-ur:
Clinical Liaison · Medical SLP, [N] yrs acute and inpatient rehab · discharge planning, payer criteria, referral relationships

or

Utilization Review · CCC-SLP · therapy documentation, medical necessity, payer criteria
items.customer-success: Customer Success / Implementation · SLP, [N] yrs · onboarding families and clinicians onto [platform type]
items.informatics: Clinical Informatics · EHR superuser and trainer · [EMR name] rollout, note templates, workflow
items.clinical-educator: Clinical Educator · AAC and dysphagia training for clinicians · [N] teams trained
items.instructional-design: Instructional Designer · adult learning from [N] yrs of clinician training · Rise, Storyline
items.data-analysis: Healthcare Analyst · outcome data, SQL, Tableau · [N] yrs clinical, CCC-SLP
items.project-management: Project Coordinator · ran programs across [N] sites · CAPM in progress
items.content-marketing: Health Content Writer · [N] yrs translating clinical ideas for families and staff
items.sales-bd: Clinical Specialist, Sales · [N] yrs recommending and implementing [device type]
items.research-coordinator: Clinical Research Coordinator · CCC-SLP · consent, protocol adherence, follow-up scheduling
items.leadership: Clinical Manager · SLP · scheduling, coverage, audits, supervision of CFs

blocks.text: Four headlines that say "will take anything", all of which SLPs actually write: "Transitioning SLP", "Burnt-out SLP seeking non-clinical roles", "Aspiring instructional designer", and the stack of four unrelated titles separated by bars. A recruiter reads all of them as someone who has not decided. Pick one target, or two that belong together, and let the rest of the map wait.

blocks.title: Before you touch the headline
blocks.text: Turn off "Share profile updates with your network" (Settings, Visibility, then Visibility of your LinkedIn activity). Otherwise the first fix below announces itself to everyone you are connected to, and in a department of six people that includes your lead. Do the edits from a personal laptop on a personal email, never the district one. And you are allowed a LinkedIn: half your colleagues have one, and a profile is not a resignation.
Four fixes, in order

items: Rewrite the headline: target-role words first, one line of bridge credibility with a number, credential last. Ten minutes, and it is the change with the largest reach, since the headline rides along on every comment and connection request you make.
Reorder your pinned skills so the target-role terms sit in the top slots and the clinical ones stay further down. Five minutes, and recruiters filter searches on exactly this field.
Rewrite About as three short first-person paragraphs: the bridge claim with a number, two translated accomplishments, then where you are heading and what you have already done to get ready.
Translate the top three bullets under each recent role, using the same three questions from 3.2, and leave the rest alone.

Open a private browser window, search your target title plus your city the way a recruiter would, and see how far down you appear. Then search the target title plus CCC-SLP and write down the names of three people who have already made this move.

Open ten profiles of people who hold your target title and read only their certification and course sections. Whatever appears on seven of them is worth having. Whatever appears on one is what somebody sold them.
Follow five companies from your list and join one group for the field, so the feed starts showing you their openings and their people instead of the caseload discourse.

blocks.title: Do not scrub the clinician out
blocks.text: A profile with a hole where a decade should be raises more questions than a translated one, and at speech-tech and health-tech companies the license is the qualification rather than the obstacle. Never change a title, a date or a role to something it was not. Fabrication is the one screening flag nobody recovers from, and your résumé and profile will be read side by side.

blocks.title: Everything you post sits under your name
blocks.text: A recruiter who finds you reads the last ten things you commented on. A post about the caseload, a reply venting about administration, a like on someone else's exit rant: each one answers the retention question for them before you get to. Use LinkedIn the way you'd speak in a conference room with the hiring manager in it, and keep the venting for the closed groups.

The positive version, if you are aiming at content, instructional design or a clinical-education role: one or two plain pieces about something you know cold, such as how dysphagia documentation actually gets written on a unit, or what makes an AAC rollout stick after the SLP leaves. A clinician writing plainly about the work is credible in a way a career changer rarely is. Post nothing for engagement, and nothing you would not want a hiring manager to read first.

takeaways: Your profile does two jobs: it corroborates the résumé, and it is how recruiters find you in the first place.
Headline, About, titles and pinned skills are the fields recruiters search, so the target-role vocabulary has to live in them.
Headline first, then the skills reorder, then About, then the top three bullets per role.
Search your own target title in a private window to see whether you are findable, then find three people who have already made the move.
Translate the history and never delete or relabel it. At speech-tech companies the clinical credential is the asset.

tldr: One documented search took over 500 applications without referrals. The people who moved faster had someone on the inside, and getting one is a twenty-minute task you have already practised.

blocks.text: You can be the best of two hundred and forty-two strangers, or you can be the person somebody already mentioned. The second is not fair, and it is how most of these moves actually happened.

blocks.text: That 500 number belongs to somebody who got there, landed a fully remote role and now earns twenty thousand more than she did as an SLP. The volume was the tax she paid for having no referrals.
Three habits that do most of the work

items: **Apply inside 48 hours.** Postings get most of their real attention in the first day or two. A tailored application on day one beats a perfect one on day nine.

**Check for an in before you hit submit.** Search the company on LinkedIn for anyone from your program, anyone with CCC-SLP in their history, anyone you have ever met. If one exists, message them first and apply second. If none exists, apply anyway and note it in the tracker.

**Message one person at the company, the same day.** Not the recruiter. Someone doing the job you applied for, ideally a former clinician. Say you applied, say the one specific thing that made you want the role, ask one question.
**Turn every conversation into a name.** At the end of any informational interview, ask who else they would talk to if they were you. That question is where a network comes from.

blocks.text: You already wrote the message in Module 2, and about one in four of them gets no answer, so three sent is usually two conversations.
What to ask for, and when

Do not ask for a referral in a first message. Ask for twenty minutes about their work, because referrals come at the end of a conversation that already happened, and they are usually offered rather than requested.

A stranger's no to a referral is rational, and knowing why makes the ask less personal. Referring you means putting their own name behind your work, sight unseen, and most people will not do that for someone they spoke to once. After a real conversation it is a different bet, and at many companies a referral that gets hired pays the referrer a bonus, so a loose acquaintance saying "I've talked to her, she seemed serious" costs them nothing and might pay. That is also why a referral works when you sit under the posted requirements: it is how a résumé gets read after the screen would have dropped it.

blocks.title: After a good conversation
blocks.text: This was genuinely useful, thank you. Two things before I let you go. Is there anyone else you'd talk to if you were me? And if a [role] opens on your team, would you be open to me sending you the posting?

That second question is the referral ask in the least awkward form I have found: a yes or no about a hypothetical, easy to agree to, and it gives you permission to come back. One more, near the end: what other companies do work like yours? Three names from someone inside is a better list than an hour of searching.

blocks.title: Why this works better for us than for most
blocks.text: Former SLPs are unusually willing to answer other SLPs, which is part of why the response rate is as high as it is. The exit threads are full of people offering to talk, and the ones who made it out tend to remember who answered them. You are not cold-messaging strangers. You are messaging people who were you two years ago.

takeaways: Applications without referrals is the expensive route: one documented search took over 500.
Apply inside 48 hours and message someone doing the job the same day.
Never ask for a referral in a first message. Ask for twenty minutes, then ask who else you should talk to.
About one in four messages gets no answer, so three sent is usually two conversations.

tldr: Two live conversations at any time is enough. Keep them warm with one short update a month, and they turn into referrals without you asking.

blocks.text: Most networking advice assumes you want a network. What you want is two or three people who know what you are looking for and would forward you a posting, which is a much smaller job.
The maintenance is smaller than you think
One message a month, per person, with one job: remind them you exist and show that you did something since last time.

blocks.title: The monthly update
blocks.text: Hi [name], quick update since we talked. I [built the thing / finished the certificate / had a first interview at X]. Still aiming at [role type]. If anything crosses your desk I'd love to hear about it. Hope [specific thing they mentioned] went well.
That is four sentences and ninety seconds. The last one matters most, because remembering the thing they told you is what separates a relationship from a mailing list.

Twice, the update becomes an ask. When the artifact from Module 5 exists, send it: "would you look at this and tell me what a hiring manager would say?" is a small, flattering job, and it puts your work in front of the person most likely to pass it on. And the week you switch from building to applying, one message to everyone you have spoken to: I'm applying now, for [title], and if you hear of one I'd be grateful for a nudge. That is the message referrals actually come from.
When somebody goes quiet
They are busy, and it is not about you. Send one follow-up after two weeks, then let it rest, and come back in six months with something new to say.
And it does not stop when you land. A note twice a year to the people who helped keeps them from becoming strangers again, and it is your insurance if the new job turns out to be the wrong one.

blocks.title: The thing that surprises people
blocks.text: The conversation that produces the job is usually not the one you expected. In the documented transitions, the useful introduction tends to come third or fourth hand, from someone who was not obviously connected to the role at all. Which is an argument for keeping two warm rather than chasing the perfect one.

action.label: Two are warm
action.prompt: Pick the two most promising people from your tracker and send each of them a monthly update this week. Four sentences, ninety seconds, ending with a question about something they told you.
action.done: Two warm. That is the network. It does not need to be bigger than this.

takeaways: Two live conversations is enough, because what you need is a couple of people who would forward you a posting rather than a network.
One four-sentence update a month keeps a conversation warm.
Silence means a busy month, not a closed door. One follow-up, then let it rest.
The introduction that works is usually third or fourth hand, which is why two warm beats one perfect.

tldr: Most SLPs distrust recruiters, and clinical staffing agencies earned that. An in-house recruiter at a company you want is a different job: they get paid when a req closes, so a candidate who fits one is useful to them. Message when a role is live, follow up once at eight days, then stop.

blocks.text: The word recruiter means something specific and unpleasant to most SLPs, and the threads are blunt about it.
No recruiters ever. Never ever.

That reputation was earned by clinical staffing and contract agencies, whose business is placing bodies in caseloads at a margin. An in-house recruiter at a health-tech company is doing a different job. They have a req to fill this quarter, their success is measured on closing it, and a candidate who clearly fits is the most useful thing that can land in their inbox. One of the documented transitions in this course happened that way, when a recruiter found a self-taught SLP on LinkedIn and she ended up at $93,000.
When to message one, and when not to

items: Message when there is a live posting you match on most of the requirement lines. That gives them something to do with you.
Do not send a cold keep me in mind note. There is no req attached, so there is nothing for them to act on and no reason to remember it.
Say the target title in the first line. Recruiters read for a role, not for a person.
Name the clinical background as an asset rather than apologising for it, especially at any company selling into hospitals or schools.

blocks.text: Vet them. A recruiter who answers "I want out of clinical work" with three SNF contracts and a PRN school posting has told you what they sell, and you can stop replying. The useful ones are narrow: there are recruiters who place only into health IT, only into device companies' clinical teams, only into learning and development. One of those covers thirty companies you could not reach on your own, and it costs nothing to connect with two of them now, with no pitch, before you need them. A cold "keep me in mind" message is still a waste; a connection without a message is a different thing.
Two messages worth sending
When a role is live, the person who decides is usually findable. One line of proof and one ask, and it goes to the hiring manager, not the recruiter.

blocks.title: The note to a hiring manager when a role is live
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], does the [title] role posted on [LinkedIn / your careers page] report to you? I've spent [N] years as an SLP in [setting], and [one specific, verifiable thing: trained fourteen clinicians through an EMR rollout / ran a caseload of 62 across three sites / built the dysphagia protocol the unit still uses]. I've applied. If you're the person hiring for it, I'd like the chance to talk.

[Your name]

And when a recruiter says you're not qualified, that is the start of a conversation, not the end of one. Name the gap, name what you'd do about it by the interview date, and ask a question they can say yes to.

blocks.title: When a recruiter says you're not qualified
blocks.text:
Thanks for being straight with me. I don't have [Salesforce / Articulate / SQL] yet. If I complete [a named course] before the interview date, would you be comfortable putting me forward? My [N] years in [setting] cover [the two requirements you do meet], and I learn tools fast because I've had to.

If the answer is still no, I'd value one line on what would change it, and when it's reasonable to check back.
The follow-up, which is where most people quit

One follow-up, eight days after the first message. It has to add something rather than repeat the ask, which usually means a line about the artifact you built or a specific question about the role. Then stop. A second follow-up does not increase your odds and it does change how you are remembered.

Hi [name], following up on [role] from last week. Since I wrote, I put together [the artifact, in six words] which is close to what the posting describes under [requirement line]. Happy to send it over if it is useful. Either way, is that req still open?
blocks.note: The last question is doing the work. It is easy to answer, and the answer tells you whether to keep going.

blocks.title: What silence means here
blocks.text: About one in four asks gets no reply, and with recruiters the rate is worse, because reqs get frozen and pipelines fill before anyone updates a posting. Silence is almost always about the req and almost never about you.

items: Open the tracker and find anyone you messaged eight or more days ago.
Send one follow-up each, adding one new thing.
Mark them closed. No third message.

takeaways: Clinical staffing agencies earned the distrust. In-house recruiters at your target companies are a different job with a different incentive.
Only message about a live req. A cold keep me in mind note gives them nothing to act on.
Lead with the target title, and name the clinical background as the asset it is at any company selling into healthcare or schools.
One follow-up at eight days, and it has to add something new. There is no second follow-up.
Frozen reqs cause most of the silence, so read it as timing rather than a verdict.
